frameworks.name: Close Rate to Pricing Ladder
frameworks.definition: A tiered mapping of close rates (sales conversion percentages) to pricing multipliers that determines how much a business is underpriced relative to its market-clearing price point.

claims.text: When close rate on a sales offer reaches 80%+ (four out of five prospects purchasing), the business is typically underpriced by 3-4x, based on Alex Hormozi's multi-year data collection across his portfolio companies.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Direct sales with salesperson (in-person, phone, or Zoom)
Close rate measured as percentage of qualified prospects who buy
claims.mechanism: High close rate signals that price-raising headroom exists because demand vastly exceeds supply at the current price point.
bounded_by: Assumes selling mechanisms (education, value demonstration) are already in place pre-pitch
Does not apply to SaaS/unlimited-scale businesses where gross margin and growth rate have inverse relationship

claims.text: In the 30-40% close rate range for service businesses with established pre-pitch education (content, proof, consultation), pricing is already market-clearing and should not be raised further without improving sales motion.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Sales motion includes consumer education prior to pitch
Close call focused on personalization, not pitch/spiel
claims.mechanism: Market-clearing price is reached when sales motion is optimized and prospects arrive pre-educated; further price increases without motion improvement will reduce close rate below equilibrium.

numbers.axis: Close rate and pricing optimization stage

anchors.region: 30-40% close rate with proper education motion

bounded_by: Only applies when pre-pitch education and sales motion are in place
If motion is absent, 30-40% close rate indicates avatar/sales process issues that should be fixed before pricing adjustment

claims.text: Below 30% close rate (less than one in three prospects converting), the constraint is almost always avatar or sales motion quality, not pricing. Alex Hormozi diagnoses and fixes these two factors before considering price changes.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Low close rates reflect misalignment between prospect and offer (avatar mismatch) or execution quality (sales motion mismatch), not pricing; raising prices on a broken sales motion compounds the problem.
bounded_by: Exception: SaaS and unlimited-scale software businesses, where pricing balances gross margin against growth rate independently

claims.text: Service businesses (80% of all businesses, per Hormozi) are inherently unscalable and have only one pricing direction: upward. The compounding cycle works as follows: higher prices → better reputation → ability to hire A-level talent → better customer results → higher demand → capacity constraints → further price increases.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Founder chooses to raise prices rather than expand capacity
claims.mechanism: Price increases force capacity constraint that signals scarcity and quality, enabling hiring of better talent (due to higher margins), which improves delivery, which compounds reputation, which increases demand, which refills the funnel at higher prices. The inverse (competing on price) creates a vicious cycle of lower margins, worse talent, worse customers, declining reputation.

numbers.axis: Service business pricing and growth dynamic

bounded_by: Does not apply to SaaS or software with unlimited unit economics
Requires founder discipline to maintain focus on quality and not chase volume

claims.text: For SaaS and unlimited-scale software businesses (approximately 5% of businesses), pricing decisions must balance two opposing forces: raising price increases gross margin but decreases growth rate; lowering price increases growth but reduces per-unit margin. The optimization is to maximize both simultaneously.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: SaaS or unlimited-scale software business model
Zero or near-zero marginal cost per unit
claims.mechanism: In software, unit economics are decoupled from delivery labor, so pricing affects only customer acquisition (lower price → higher volume) and margin retention (higher price → more reinvestment capital), creating a true trade-off that unscalable businesses do not face.

numbers.axis: Business type distribution and pricing strategy

bounded_by: This inverse relationship (margin vs. growth) does not apply to service businesses where margin improvements enable talent and reputation gains that actually increase growth

examples.text: A service business founder running at $100 price point with 80%+ close rate could test raising price to $300-400 based on the 3-4x multiplier, expecting minimal conversion loss if sales motion and proof infrastructure are in place. The key is ensuring prospects are pre-educated before the close call.

Service business pricing is a compounding loop: as prices rise, the founder can afford higher-quality talent, which delivers better results, which builds reputation, which creates demand far exceeding capacity. This forces further price increases to manage demand. The alternative (competing on lower price) creates the opposite effect: worse margins attract worse talent, worse talent produces mediocre results, mediocre results require volume to survive, volume at low prices shrinks margins further, creating a downward spiral.

practices.text: Before raising prices on a low-performing sales funnel, first diagnose and fix avatar fit and sales motion quality. Only after those levers are optimized should pricing be adjusted upward.

In service businesses, when facing a capacity constraint, raise prices rather than hire more staff. The price increase buys time to systematize delivery and improves margins that enable hiring A-level talent.
